slides.title: Conditional probability and Bayes’ rule
bullets: Lecture 02 · Probability Notebook
How probabilities change when we learn that something happened

slides.title: Conditioning on an event
bullets: Learning that B happened rules out every outcome outside B
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), defined only when P(B) > 0
Read P(A | B) as “the probability of A given B”
One fair die: P(six | even) = (1/6) / (1/2) = 1/3

slides.title: A conditional probability is a probability
bullets: For a fixed B with P(B) > 0, P(· | B) satisfies every axiom
So the usual rules carry over: P(A′ | B) = 1 − P(A | B)
With equally likely outcomes: P(A | B) = |A ∩ B| / |B|
P(A | B) and P(B | A) answer different questions and usually differ

slides.title: The multiplication rule
bullets: Rearranging the definition: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) · P(A | B)
Either order works: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B | A)
Chain rule: P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A) · P(B | A) · P(C | A ∩ B)
Two cards without replacement, both aces: (4/52) · (3/51) = 1/221

slides.title: Independence
bullets: A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B)
If P(B) > 0 this says P(A | B) = P(A): learning B changes nothing about A
Two fair dice: “first die shows 6” and “sum is 7” are independent
Independence is a fact about probabilities, not about physical causes

slides.title: Disjoint is not independent
bullets: Disjoint events with P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0 are never independent
Disjoint means P(A ∩ B) = 0, but then P(A) · P(B) > 0
Learning that B happened tells you A did not: that is strong dependence

slides.title: The law of total probability
bullets: A partition: disjoint events B₁, B₂, … that together make up Ω
P(A) = P(A | B₁)P(B₁) + P(A | B₂)P(B₂) + …, one term for each piece
Simplest partition: B and B′, so P(A) = P(A | B)P(B) + P(A | B′)P(B′)
Strategy: split a hard question into easy cases, then add them up

slides.title: Bayes’ rule
bullets: Reverses a conditional: from P(A | B) to P(B | A)
P(B | A) = P(A | B) · P(A) / P(B)
Denominator by total probability: P(A) = P(A | B)P(B) + P(A | B′)P(B′)
Vocabulary: prior P(B), likelihood P(A | B), posterior P(B | A)

slides.title: Diagnostic tests and base rates
bullets: Prevalence P(D), sensitivity P(+ | D), false-positive rate P(+ | D′)
The patient wants P(D | +), and that needs all three numbers
1% prevalence, 99% sensitivity, 5% false positives: P(D | +) = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%
Base-rate fallacy: ignoring P(D) and reading P(+ | D) as if it were P(D | +)

slides.title: Natural frequencies
bullets: Out of 10,000 people, 100 have the condition and 99 of them test positive
Of the 9,900 without it, 5% = 495 also test positive
So 99 of the 594 positives are sick: 99/594 = 1/6
A rare condition means most positives come from the large healthy group

slides.title: Tree diagrams
bullets: First level: the partition (sick or healthy), labelled with prior probabilities
Second level: the test result, labelled with conditional probabilities
Multiply along a path to get the probability of that path
Add the paths that end in the same result; Bayes divides one path by that total

slides.title: Updating twice
bullets: Yesterday’s posterior is today’s prior
A second positive, independent of the first given the true status:

slides.title: Summary
bullets: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B): keep only B, then rescale
The multiplication and chain rules build joint probabilities step by step
Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); disjoint events are not independent
Total probability splits into cases; Bayes’ rule reverses the conditional
Always ask for the base rate
